newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African motor restructuring shows mixed results.
newsitem.headline: S.African motor restructuring shows mixed results.

text.p: After a tough two years under a new development plan, South Africa's motor vehicle and components industries have shown mixed results.
Consumers have benefited from a slide of about 10 percent in real vehicle prices while a wider range of models, including the increasingly popular smaller "entry-level" cars, are available.

Exports of cars and commercial vehicles have doubled, mainly to other African states. The National Association of Automobile Manufacturers of South Africa (Naamsa) reports that exports rose to 6,207 units in the first five months of this year, compared to 3,267 in the same period last year.
Exports of components are expected to total 4.5 billion rand this year compared to just over four billion rand last year.

Although there have been job losses, they have been minimal and in some cases compensated for by jobs created by manufacturers re-entering the market, albeit in most cases merely to market and service vehicles built elsewhere.

Based on the Australian model and introduced two years ago, the motor industry development programme (MIDP) has seen import tariffs on completely built up (CBU) units fall to 57.5 percent from 115 percent nearly three years ago. Tariffs are set to drop to 40 percent by the time the programme runs out in 2002.
This has encouraged new entrants such as Korea's Hyundai Motor Co Ltd and Daewoo, America's Chrysler Corp, Daihatsu Motor Co Ltd, Peugeot SA, Renault SA and Volvo AB.

A Naamsa spokesman told Reuters that imports would this year rise to around 14 or 15 percent of total car market of 274,000 units from 12.6 percent or 35,000 units in 1996. This would probably expand to between 20 and 25 percent by 2002.

"It's a mixed picture, but, on balance, I would say that it is quite positive," said University of Cape Town economics lecturer Anthony Black, who has been monitoring the motor vehicle industry for government.

His main disappointment has been that not much rationalisation has taken place in the industry despite relatively large investments by Japan's Toyota Motor Corp and Nissan Motor Co Ltd as well as Germany's BMW AG over the last year.

"What we have not seen yet are investments on the scale of what is happening in some emerging markets like Brazil," Black said. "It is a question of market size. Brazil is serving the whole of South America."

Although South Africa's vehicle exports to the rest of Africa were significant at 70 percent of total exports, mainly to Zimbabwe, the African market was not large enough to warrant a truly world scale plant in South Africa.
But there were encouraging developments, Black said.
BMW, for example, was expanding its plant and planned to increase its exports of its new 3-series vehicles to 25,000 a year. These would largely go to non-African markets.

"The big success has been the components exports rather than the vehicle exports, although one would expect more of a lag for vehicle exports because of the bigger investments needed. We expect that those will pick up," he said.

Black said the Department of Trade and Industry and the Motor Industry Development Council were keeping a close watch on trends in the sector ahead of the mid-term review of the MIDP planned for next year.
"One of things we are monitoring is the local content, which has shown a slight decline and we expect this to continue because there is less protection," he said.
Local content in domestically assembled vehicles fell to about 53 percent first quarter of 1997 compared to 56 percent for 1996 as a whole.
